newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania vote hit by violence, ballot tampering.
newsitem.headline: Albania vote hit by violence, ballot tampering.

text.p: A local election official was shot and killed in southern Albania during voting in Sunday's general election, the first person to die in violence on election day.

A spokesman for the Interior Ministry in the capital Tirana indentified the victim as Burhan Misiri, the chief electoral official in a village near the town of Fier. "The crime was politically motivated," he told Reuters.

The spokesman added a policeman was injured by gunfire during the melee. He said the victim was a member of President Sali Berisha's ruling Democratic Party while the chief suspect had links to the Socialist Party challenging it for power.
Details of the incident were sketchy and it was not clear whether Misiri had been shot at the polling station.
Fatos Klosi, vice chairman of the Central Electoral Commission (CEC) organising the vote, told reporters at a press conference in Tirana: "He was killed on the job."
Voting in Albania's general election, called to end months of unrest sparked by the collapse of shady investment schemes, had been proceeding with only minor incidents until mid-day.
Both the Democrats and the Socialists complained of irregularities, mainly voters left off registration lists or being intimidated by armed thugs.

According to a report by the Italian-led security force, despatched to Albania to help contain the unrest, armed gunmen stole all ballot papers in a polling station near the northern port town of Durres shortly after the station opened at 7 a.m.
The spokesman said the ballots were later returned by local police and voting resumed.

In the northern district of Malesia e Madhe, local election commission members had refused to move polling stations from private houses to local schools or other public buildings as demanded by central authorities, Klosi of the CEC said.
"They refused to obey the orders," he said, adding that he could not say whether the vote had been suspended.
Because of Albania's obsolete telecommunications, information from remote villages is sparse and slow in coming.

The poor state of Albania's roads poses additional problems for election officials and the 500-strong team of international observers monitoring the vote for the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE).

The official news agency ATA reported that armed gangs had forced their way into several polling stations in the town of Lezhe, 60 km (40 miles) north of Tirana, and forced election officials at gunpoint to stuff the ballot boxes.
The report could not immediately be confirmed.

In the central district of Mat, no voting was taking place as ballot papers had not been delivered. The OSCE had to reprint papers for 10 districts 48 hours before the vote after election officials complained of errors.

CEC chairman Kristaq Kume appealed to Albanians in a broadcast carried on state television to vote in peace. He said the shooting was "an event which must be denounced and amounts to an attack not only on him and his family but on all of us".
The situation in the capital Tirana remained calm throughout the day and correspondents visiting polling stations around the city had no reports of serious irregularities.

Albania's fourth multi-party elections since the fall of communism in 1990 are being held under a state of emergency imposed on March 2. A country-wide 10 p.m. to 5 a.m. curfew has been suspended just for polling day.
